claude.sample_unit: generated patient protocols (25 MTB cases x 2 prompting approaches) expert-annotated

links.outcome: Whether automatic metric gains predict expert-assessed clinical safety of deployed LLM configuration
links.effect: One-shot prompting improved automatic metrics across all 8 models, yet protocols with at least one critical error doubled (10/25, 40% vs 5/25, 20%); metrics were insufficient proxies for clinical safety.
links.quote: Surface-level metric gains were, therefore, insufficient proxies for clinical safety.

links.outcome: Interannotator agreement among independent expert annotators using a defined taxonomy and training
links.effect: Gwet AC1 was 0.72 (95% CI 0.67-0.76) for all errors and 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96) for critical errors.
links.quote: Almost perfect agreement [ 44 ] was reached on critical errors (Gwet AC1=0.94, 95% CI 0.92 to 0.96), which supports the validity of the critical error rate as the safety-relevant outcome of this study.

links.outcome: Overreliance and automation bias in clinician review of AI drafts
links.effect: Reviewer vigilance was not tested. Authors caution automation bias may compromise error detection, and low perceived editing effort may reflect it. No with/without-AI comparison was done.
links.quote: This study did not test reviewer vigilance under realistic workflow conditions, and future work should assess error detection rates under ecologically valid review conditions before clinical deployment.

links.outcome: Effect of one-shot exemplar prompting on critical and factual errors in generated protocols
links.effect: Critical-error protocols rose from 5/25 (20%) under zero-shot to 10/25 (40%) under one-shot; factual errors became dominant (69/145, 48%); 18 annotations across 6 protocols showed exemplar contamination.
links.quote: The increase in critical errors under A2 was driven by exemplar contamination (18 annotations across 6 protocols).

links.outcome: Readability and complexity of LLM-generated patient protocols versus expert-written gold standard
links.effect: WSTF4 remained in the medium difficulty range (10-12), about grade 10 or higher. DistilBERT complexity was 4.10-4.78 versus 2.79 for the gold standard.
links.quote: DistilBERT-based complexity assessments showed that all generated texts remained far from the gold standard (2.79) within a similar complexity range (4.10‐4.78), with no systematic differences between the approaches.

links.outcome: Frequency of errors in AI-generated drafts requiring clinician verification
links.effect: Experts found 253 errors in 16% (230/1420) of paragraphs; 20% (A1) to 40% (A2) of protocols had at least one critical error, so clinician verification remains required.
links.quote: A critical error rate of 20%‐40% precludes clinical applicability of the selected model under the conditions tested.

links.outcome: Critical errors in AI-drafted patient protocols that could reach patients unreviewed
links.effect: Critical errors bearing risk of patient harm appeared in 5/25 (20%) zero-shot and 10/25 (40%) one-shot protocols.
links.quote: However, these outputs require mandatory review by experts with domain expertise sufficient to verify clinical claims against the source protocol (internal) and general medical knowledge (external).

links.outcome: Automatic metrics versus expert safety errors
links.effect: A2 improved automatic metrics, but ≥1 critical error doubled for Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct: 10/25, 40% vs 5/25, 20%.
links.quote: However, expert usability evaluation of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct showed the opposite picture: the proportion of protocols containing at least 1 critical error doubled under A2 (10/25, 40% vs 5/25, 20%) compared with A1, and the dominant error type shifted from language (40/108, 37%) errors to factual errors (69/145, 48%).

links.outcome: Critical errors in patient-facing AI protocols
links.effect: ≥1 critical error occurred in 20% (n=5) of A1 and 40% (n=10) of A2 protocols.
links.quote: The proportion of protocols with ≥1 critical error was 20% (n=5) for A1 and 40% (n=10) for A2.

links.effect: Exemplar contamination drove increased A2 critical errors: 18 annotations across 6 protocols.
links.quote: The increase in critical errors under A2 was driven by exemplar contamination (18 annotations across 6 protocols).

links.effect: WSTF4 stayed medium difficulty, requiring at least grade 10 comprehension; complexity was 4.10-4.78 versus gold standard 2.79.
links.quote: Despite significant WSTF4 improvements under A2, scores across both approaches remained in the medium difficulty range (10-12), which corresponds to an approximate comprehension requirement of at least grade 10.
